要旨

To be drafted.

Abstract

During crises, everyday essentials can disappear from retail shelves within days even when physical supply remains intact and most consumers neither panic nor hoard. Existing accounts of how individual consumer behavior generates these market-wide shortages remain incomplete. Micro-level studies measure real consumer reactions, implicitly treating shortages as a simple aggregation of independent actions rather than modeling how purchases deplete shelves and shared warnings alter what other consumers encounter. Macro-level models, conversely, reproduce aggregate shortages, but rely on divergent, empirically ungrounded rules that typically build in extreme shifts such as panic or heavy stockpiling. Viewing consumer behavior and the surrounding environment as mutually shaping, this thesis bridges these levels by combining two scenario-based online studies in Japan with an agent-based simulation grounded in their findings, examining how empirically observed buying and information-sharing tendencies interact to produce market-wide shortages. Study 1 (N = 284, rice, January 2026) and a preregistered Study 2 (N = 536, toilet paper and laundry detergent, June 2026) measured how consumers respond to seeing a nearly empty store shelf or a social media post about a shortage. Across both studies, consumers who expected future supply to be less stable reported modestly greater willingness to buy and to warn family, friends, and acquaintances (r = .18 to .20). Posting publicly on social media, however, remained rare and showed inconsistent links with supply expectations (r = .05, p = .42 in Study 1; r = .19, p < .001 in Study 2). Drawing qualitatively on these tendencies, Study 3 simulated a spatially structured retail market in which consumers shop at local neighborhood stores with limited stock and pass shortage warnings privately over a small-world network. Consumers bought at most a single unit and raised their buying probability only slightly upon hearing warnings, with no public broadcasting. Under these restrained rules, small simultaneous increases in how readily consumers acted on warnings and how often they passed them along markedly accelerated stock depletion—provided a small share of personal ties reached distant neighborhoods. These findings illustrate a plausible mechanism by which rapid, market-wide shortages could emerge when local store stockouts and privately shared warnings feed into each other across long-range personal ties.

1. Introduction

This thesis examines panic buying, in which everyday essentials suddenly disappear from retail shelves during a crisis. In late February 2020, after social media rumors claimed that Japan’s toilet paper supply depended on China and would be disrupted by COVID-19 lockdowns (Cato et al., 2021), toilet paper vanished from supermarkets and drugstores across Japan within days. Supermarket sales of toilet paper rose to about three times the level of the previous year on February 27, peaked at about 5.9 times on February 28, and fell to about 1.2 times by March 8–9 (Iizuka et al., 2022, Figure 1). Independently, the Statistics Bureau of Japan (2020) reported that household spending on tissue and toilet paper on February 28 was about 6.6 times the daily average for February 2019. Even as retail shelves emptied, however, production capacity and manufacturers’ inventories remained sufficient. Addressing the rumors, the Japan Household Paper Industry Association stated on February 28 that almost all toilet paper was made domestically without relying on Chinese raw materials, and specified a domestic share of about 98% on March 2 (Japan Household Paper Industry Association, 2020a, 2020b). On March 3, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (2020) urged calm buying, reporting that manufacturers held roughly three weeks of national consumption in stock and had doubled daily deliveries since February 28. A comparable episode occurred in the United Kingdom in late March 2012, after media reports of an industrial dispute involving fuel tanker drivers and a planned strike ballot. Within two days, gas stations began running out of stock, and panic buying of fuel spread nationwide. Yet no strike ever took place and the fuel supply chain was never disrupted; by early April, the shortage had largely subsided (Upton & Nuttall, 2014). Similar episodes have been documented across countries and everyday essentials, including salt in China after the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident (Wei et al., 2011) and household products during the early COVID-19 pandemic (Keane & Neal, 2021; O’Connell et al., 2021; Yuen et al., 2020). Together, these cases show how demand can surge abruptly, deplete local retail stocks within days even when production and upstream supply remain intact, and then subside once immediate demand is met. Because such shortages disrupt retail distribution and leave households unable to obtain everyday essentials, understanding why they occur remains an important question.

1.1. Micro-Level Explanations

Why do such shortages erupt when physical supply remains intact? Media coverage and early academic accounts have commonly framed these episodes as “panic buying,” attributing them to extreme fear, irrational overreaction, selfish hoarding, or herd mentality (Arafat et al., 2020; Brackley & Wells, 2025; Loxton et al., 2020; Sim et al., 2020; for critiques of this framing, see Lindell, 2024; Ntontis et al., 2022). Following a similar focus on individual vulnerability, much empirical research has used cross-sectional surveys to identify individual predictors of who buys more during a crisis. These studies link higher self-reported buying to negative emotions, such as anxiety and anticipated regret, and to perceived threat, meaning judgments about how likely people are to be affected and how serious the consequences would be (Bentall et al., 2021; Chua et al., 2021; Laato et al., 2020). Other studies have focused on stable personal characteristics. Garbe et al. (2020) found that conscientiousness predicted stockpiling directly, whereas emotionality in the HEXACO personality framework (a trait encompassing fearfulness, anxiety, dependence, and sentimentality) was associated with stockpiling indirectly through perceived threat. Extending this approach, Bentall et al. (2021) examined a different set of psychological characteristics, including paranoia, authoritarianism, and analytic reasoning.

Empirical evidence, however, challenges this picture of an irrational, panicking, or hoarding public. Household scanner records from the 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Japan (Hori & Iwamoto, 2014) and the first COVID-19 wave in the United Kingdom (O’Connell et al., 2021) show that aggregate demand spikes were driven mainly by a larger share of households choosing to buy within the same window. In the UK records, average quantities per trip increased only slightly, indicating that extreme purchases were not the main driver of aggregate demand. Consistent with these transaction records, nationally representative surveys in the United Kingdom and Ireland found that roughly three-quarters of adults reported minimal excess buying during the early pandemic (Bentall et al., 2021). Crisis researchers have likewise challenged the label “panic buying,” arguing that extra buying often reflects ordinary precaution and preparedness rather than acute emotional panic (Lindell, 2024; Ntontis et al., 2022). Throughout this thesis, we retain the established term panic buying without implying that consumers are panicking. Widespread belief in false rumors does not fit the evidence either. During Japan’s 2020 shortage, official reassurances were available on the day sales peaked, Twitter posts correcting the rumor spread more widely than the rumor itself, and only 6.2% of respondents to a government survey believed a shortage actually existed (Iizuka et al., 2022; Japan Household Paper Industry Association, 2020a). To explain this pattern, Iizuka et al. proposed pluralistic ignorance, in which people reject a rumor themselves yet still buy because they expect others to believe it and empty the shelves. Such findings direct attention to expectations about other consumers’ behavior. While personality traits and general tendencies toward anxiety or precaution can help explain who buys extra, on their own they cannot explain why demand for one everyday essential suddenly rises and then falls during a particular crisis.

To address what changes during a crisis, other surveys and experiments have focused on situational triggers. Often framed around a stimulus-organism-response model, these studies examine how empty shelves, other consumers’ purchases, media coverage, or shortage rumors raise perceived scarcity or threat and, in turn, increase purchase intention (Chua et al., 2021; Islam et al., 2021; Prentice et al., 2022). In this thesis, we use the term shortage information for information that a product is, or may soon become, unavailable, which consumers can encounter firsthand at a nearly empty shelf or secondhand through another person or a social media post. Across empirical studies, associations with buying are positive but graded rather than abrupt, ranging from moderate cross-sectional correlations with perceived scarcity (e.g., latent r = .45 with a small direct path of \(\beta = .14\) in Chua et al., 2021) to small effects of concrete shortage information in scenario experiments (r = .16 to .31 in Ma & Liao, 2022) and post-disaster surveys (partial r = .11 after the 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Kurihara et al., 2012). Although this approach helps explain why an individual becomes more likely to buy at a specific time, these studies generally treat shortage information and other consumers’ behavior as external inputs and focus only on individual reactions. In a demand-driven shortage, however, consumers also create the information that others encounter. A shelf is empty because earlier shoppers bought from it, and a consumer learns about a shortage from home because someone chose to pass the information along. Studying responses alone therefore leaves unexplained how purchases and information sharing generate the conditions that prompt further buying.

Explaining how a demand-driven shortage emerges requires a micro-macro framework in which consumer behavior and the surrounding environment continuously reshape each other (Schelling, 1978; Yamagishi, 1992). A market-wide shortage can emerge even when no individual intends to create one. Buying in anticipation of empty shelves helps empty them, giving other consumers a reason to buy sooner and making the initial expectation self-fulfilling. Individual actions change the environment through two coupled channels, altering both objective and social reality (Yamagishi, 1992). First, a purchase physically reduces local retail inventory, leaving less stock for subsequent shoppers to see and buy. Second, private sharing passes shortage information to people a consumer knows, shaping their expectations before they visit a store. Because these two channels can reinforce one another over time, even modest changes in individual buying tendencies may accelerate stock depletion once purchases and information sharing feed back through stores and other consumers. Evaluating this possibility requires examining both information sharing and its feedback with local retail conditions.

1.2. Macro-Level and Formal Models

Whereas micro-level surveys struggle to link individual responses to market-wide shortages, studies starting from aggregate data or formal theory face the reverse problem. Although they examine information sharing, social networks, and market dynamics, many different individual rules can reproduce the same aggregate trajectory, so matching a macro pattern alone cannot establish which psychological mechanism operated (Epstein, 1999; Grimm et al., 2005). One group of studies starts from aggregate sales or patterns of information diffusion in social media and infers an individual mechanism. Iizuka et al. (2022) regressed daily supermarket sales of toilet paper during Japan’s 2020 shortage on estimated Twitter views of misinformation, corrections denying the shortage rumor, and posts reporting stores that had sold out. Because views of corrections were the strongest predictor of sales, they proposed pluralistic ignorance as the underlying mechanism. Yet mapping public tweet views directly onto sales omits physical store stockouts and household saturation, both of which can depress sales once shelves empty and households have bought, offering alternative explanations for the sharp decline after a sales peak. Moreover, the analysis infers individual psychology from aggregate time series without measuring how consumers respond to or privately share shortage information. Agent-based models of contagion face a related limitation. Studies targeting aggregate social media activity, search trends, retail indices, or epidemic curves use different individual rules, including emotional contagion on scale-free networks (Chen et al., 2022), compartments borrowed from epidemic models combined with opinion dynamics and panic driven by unmet needs (Fu et al., 2021), and binary anxiety states (Fast et al., 2015). In these three models, individual rules are assumed rather than estimated from consumer data, there are no stores that can run out of stock, and validation relies on aggregate curves.

A second group of formal models specifies elaborate individual decision rules that are assumed rather than empirically grounded in behavior measured during a crisis. Building on Iizuka et al. (2022), Miyashita et al. (2025) modeled Japan’s 2020 shortage on an online social network by combining subjective logic for opinion updating with cumulative prospect theory for decision-making. Their agents switch between normal and selfish buying using assumed parameters rather than survey estimates, and the model includes no physical stores. Similarly, economic equilibrium models derive shortage spirals from strong assumptions about consumer rationality and foresight. Noda and Teramoto (2024) modeled fully rational consumers who plan ahead and anticipate higher shopping costs, using a mean-field equilibrium model in continuous time calibrated to a pre-crisis 2015 baseline survey. Klumpp and Su (2025) showed that, once supply falls even slightly short and prices cannot adjust, fully rational households can coordinate on equilibria with heavy stockpiling, in some cases up to their storage limit. Neither model includes a network for private sharing or consumer data collected during a crisis, and both require an external shock, such as higher shopping costs or a supply shortfall, to initiate the spiral. More broadly, most formal models of panic buying assume an abrupt switch into panic or selfish buying, a sharp jump in demand, or heavy stockpiling. Such assumptions leave open whether rapid shortages can arise from the more modest individual adjustments observed in scanner records and national surveys (Bentall et al., 2021; Hori & Iwamoto, 2014; O’Connell et al., 2021).

Because neither micro-level nor macro-level studies provide a complete account on their own, an empirically grounded micro-macro approach is needed. Two agent-based modeling studies come particularly close to coupling local retail shortages with social or empirical consumer processes, yet both retain key limitations. Upton and Nuttall (2014) capture the core feedback structure in a model of UK fuel panics, where shortages and queues at local fuel stations generate shortage information that drivers pass to one another across a small-world network and that feeds back into decisions about when to refuel. However, their behavioral and communication parameters are assumed rather than grounded in consumer survey data, and drivers make a binary switch into panic. The mechanism also depends on car fuel tanks and repeated refueling, which differ from household purchases of other everyday essentials. Dulam et al. (2021a, 2021b) move toward empirical grounding by combining consumer survey data with a model of local retail stores to simulate bottled water purchases after a disaster. Yet their empirical predictors are fixed personal and household characteristics rather than responses that shift during a crisis, roughly a third of households are coded as heavy stockpilers from the outset, and media reports and rumors enter as preset external inputs rather than through consumers’ private sharing.

1.3. Overview of the Present Research

Taken together, prior explanations leave a micro-macro gap between individual consumer responses and the market-wide shortages those responses jointly produce. This gap takes three forms. First, micro-level studies measure individual responses but generally omit how purchases and information sharing create the environment faced by other consumers (Yamagishi, 1992). Second, macro-level studies reproduce aggregate patterns with individual rules that are assumed rather than measured during a crisis. Third, even the closest micro-macro simulations retain binary panic states, preset heavy stockpiling, or external media inputs that do not arise from private sharing. The field still lacks an account that qualitatively grounds both buying and private sharing rules in behavior measured during a crisis and tests whether modest buying adjustments can accelerate stock depletion through feedback between local stores and consumers. Here, empirical grounding means that observed behavioral tendencies guide the model’s rules and structure; it does not mean that its probability parameters are calibrated to survey data.

These gaps motivate the central puzzle of the present thesis. Transaction records and surveys suggest that aggregate demand can rise largely because more households buy, while many consumers make only modest adjustments. Can a minimal micro-macro mechanism generate rapid stock depletion under these behavioral constraints? Answering this question requires combining empirical measurement with formal modeling of how individual behaviors interact over time (Borsboom et al., 2021; Robinaugh et al., 2021; Smaldino, 2017). Accordingly, this thesis addresses two research questions, focusing on consumers’ subjective prospects (their expectations of whether a product will be available in the coming days). First, when consumers encounter shortage information, are more negative subjective prospects associated with stronger purchase intention and information-sharing intention? Second, can a minimal model with qualitatively grounded behavioral rules generate rapid stock depletion across stores, and under what conditions does this occur?

To answer these questions, the thesis combines two empirical studies with an agent-based simulation. Both empirical studies measure purchase intention, private and public information-sharing intentions, and subjective prospects when participants encounter shortage information firsthand at a nearly empty shelf or secondhand through a social media post. Study 1 is an exploratory scenario-based experiment conducted after Japan’s 2024–2025 rice shortage, examining the structure of these intentions and their links to manipulated and measured subjective prospects. Study 2 is a preregistered conceptual replication using toilet paper and laundry detergent during the 2026 oil supply crisis, testing whether the behavioral structure and modest associations observed in Study 1 generalize across products and crisis contexts. These studies examine responses to shortage information rather than establish the causes of the crises themselves. Study 3 then couples local retail inventories with private sharing in a minimal agent-based simulation. Its behavioral rules are qualitatively grounded in the empirical pattern of modest buying adjustments and private sharing, while its probability parameters are not calibrated to the surveys. Using single-unit purchases and a bounded, graded change in buying probability, the model tests whether feedback through local stores and private sharing can accelerate stock depletion without heavy stockpiling or a binary panic state. The empirical studies also extend evidence beyond COVID-19 to two crisis contexts and three everyday essentials in Japan, contributing to a literature in which 684 of 1,049 papers (65.2%) concerned COVID-19 in our review (see Appendix).

2. Study 1: Rice Supply News and Responses to Shortage Information

Study 1 examined how consumers respond to shortage information about rice, an everyday essential in Japanese households. Japanese consumers experienced a market-wide rice shortage from 2024 to 2025 (i.e., the Reiwa rice crisis). Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF) acknowledged a rice shortage in early summer 2024, driven by rising demand from inbound tourism and a supply shortfall caused by extreme weather in 2023 (Ohinata, 2026). Against this backdrop, consumers sharply increased their rice purchases in response to the special advisory announced by the Japan Meteorological Agency on August 8, 2024, warning of an increased risk of a major earthquake (officially known as the “Nankai Trough Earthquake Extra Information”), which led to severe disruptions in rice distribution across Japan in August and September 2024 (Fukutomi, 2024). Study 1 was conducted in January 2026, while memories of this episode were still relatively fresh.

We expected that exposure to newspaper articles reporting positive or negative prospects for future rice supply would affect consumers’ purchase intention. To test this, we manipulated subjective prospects for future rice supply by presenting real newspaper articles (see Appendix) reporting either negative or positive analyses of the future supply. We then measured purchase intention and information-sharing intention in two contexts, where participants learned of a shortage either directly (e.g., while shopping) or indirectly (e.g., from a social media post). The study was exploratory and was not preregistered.

2.1. Method

We recruited Japanese adults through the Japanese survey company Cross Marketing Inc. (https://www.cross-m.co.jp/en) in January 2026 and analyzed 284 of 575 responses (46.8% men; age M = 45.28, SD = 8.87; exclusions in Appendix). The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Graduate School of Humanities and Sociology, University of Tokyo (UTSP-25047).

Participants were randomly assigned to read two real newspaper articles that were either negative (“Shinmai, Zōsanka no Neagari,” 2025; Yasuda, 2025) or positive (“Kome Kakaku ni Sakiyasukan,” 2025; Nakazawa, 2025) about the future supply of rice (n = 165 and 119, respectively). We presented excerpts rather than full articles, selecting sentences about the future supply of rice without changing their wording, so that the two articles in each condition totaled about 540 Japanese characters (542 negative, 536 positive).

Participants then rated their subjective prospects for the future rice supply and reported their purchase intention and information-sharing intention in two contexts (see Appendix). The first involved finding the rice shelf of their usual supermarket almost empty (direct observation), and the second involved seeing a social media post with a photo of such a shelf (indirect observation). Observation context was a within-participant factor whose presentation order was counterbalanced, and each context was illustrated with a corresponding AI-generated picture (participants were explicitly told that the pictures were generated using AI; Figure 1).

Figure 1: Pictures shown in the direct observation context (left) and the indirect observation context (right) of Study 1. Both pictures were generated using AI, and participants were told so.

2.1.1. Measures

Subjective Prospects. Participants’ subjective prospects for future rice supply were measured with three 5-point scale items: how do you think the supply will change (1 = very unstable to 5 = very stable), how do you think about it (1 = very pessimistic to 5 = very optimistic), and how likely do you think a shortage like the Reiwa rice crisis will happen again (1 = very low to 5 = very high). The first and second item scores were reverse-coded so that higher values indicate more negative prospects, and we aggregated the three item scores confirming their sufficient internal consistency (Cronbach’s \(\alpha\) = .82).

Purchase Intention. Participants’ purchase intention in response to shortage information was measured in each observation context with three 5-point scale items (1 = definitely not to 5 = definitely; Table 5). In the direct observation context, participants rated whether they would buy the remaining rice at the store when they had rice left at home for a few days, for more than a week, or for more than a month. In the indirect observation context, they rated whether they would go to buy rice right away under the same three levels of household stock.

Information-sharing Intention. Participants’ information-sharing intention was measured in each observation context with three 5-point scale items on the same scale (1 = definitely not to 5 = definitely; Table 5). Two items measured private information-sharing intention in both observation contexts, one asking about telling housemates, best friends, or a romantic partner about the shortage (close relationship item) and the other asking about telling acquaintances or friends (casual relationship item).

A third item measured public information-sharing intention, asking whether participants would post about the store shortage to many unspecified people on social media in the direct observation context, or repost the social media post in the indirect observation context.

2.2. Results

2.2.1. Behavioral variables

Because the behavioral items (i.e., items to measure purchase intentions and information-sharing intentions) covered various types of responses to shortage information, we first conducted an exploratory factor analysis (minimum residual extraction with varimax rotation). Three eigenvalues exceeded 1 (4.96, 2.26 and 1.37; the fourth was 0.92), and the three factors explained 62.7% of the total variance (Table 1; see Appendix 6.2.4 for robustness checks).

The first factor was related to purchase intention. Regardless of whether participants obtained the shortage information directly or indirectly, and regardless of how much rice they had at home, six items related to purchase intention highly loaded on the first factor. The second factor was related to private information-sharing intention. Four items about privately sharing the shortage information (i.e., sharing with either close or casual relationship partners in either direct or indirect observation context) highly loaded on the second factor. The third factor was related to public information-sharing intention. Two items about publicly sharing the shortage information on social media (i.e., either in direct or indirect observation context) highly loaded on the third factor.

Following the observed factor structure, we aggregated the six purchase intention item scores (Cronbach’s \(\alpha\) = .87), four private information-sharing item scores (\(\alpha\) = .86), and two public information-sharing item scores (\(\alpha\) = .88; r = .79 between the two items), respectively.

2.2.2. Effect of the news condition

The manipulation was successful. Participants in the negative prospects condition (M = 4.05, SD = 0.66) held more negative subjective prospects about the future supply of rice than participants in the positive prospects condition (M = 3.12, SD = 0.76): \(t\)(231) = 10.75, p < .001, d = 1.32.

However, the prospects manipulation did not have significant effects on purchase intention (Mneg [SD] = 2.79 [0.83] vs. Mpos [SD] = 2.73 [0.78], t[263] = 0.64, p = .521, d = 0.08) and public information-sharing intention (Mneg [SD] = 1.72 [0.85] vs. Mpos [SD] = 1.70 [0.75], t[270] = 0.18, p = .853, d = 0.02; see Table 10 in the Appendix). The effect was significant for private information-sharing intention (Mneg [SD] = 2.91 [0.88] vs. Mpos [SD] = 2.70 [0.85], t[258] = 2.02, p = .044, d = 0.24).

2.2.3. Subjective prospects and behavioral intentions

For exploratory purposes, we computed the Pearson’s product-moment correlations between subjective prospects and behavioral intention scores collapsing the newspaper conditions (Table 11 in the Appendix gives the full correlation matrix). The subjective prospects \(\times\) purchase intention correlation was significant (r[282] = .18, 95% CI [.07, .29], p = .002), suggesting that participants with more negative subjective prospects were more willing to buy rice. The subjective prospects \(\times\) private information-sharing intention correlation was also significant (r[282] = .18, 95% CI [.06, .29], p = .003), suggesting that participants with more negative subjective prospects were more willing to share the shortage information privately. The subjective prospects \(\times\) public information-sharing intention correlation was not significant (r[282] = .05, 95% CI [−.07, .16], p = .420). The correlations did not differ between the news conditions (Fisher’s r-to-z test; Table 12 in the Appendix).

2.3. Discussion

As intended, participants who read negative articles reported more negative subjective prospects about the rice supply than those who read positive articles. Although the newspaper manipulation affected private information-sharing intention, it did not affect purchase intention or public information-sharing intention. Collapsing across the two conditions, participants with more negative subjective prospects reported higher purchase intention and higher private information-sharing intention. Together, these results suggest that negative subjective prospects about supply are associated with stronger purchase intention and private information-sharing intention.

Several factors may explain why the manipulation did not produce larger differences in behavioral intentions. First, the contrast appears to have been between more and less negative prospects rather than between negative and positive prospects. Subjective prospects leaned negative across the entire sample, remaining near the scale midpoint even in the positive prospects condition. Because the study was conducted shortly after the 2024–2025 rice shortage, when rice prices remained high (Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, 2026), the positive articles may only have made participants’ subjective prospects less negative rather than positive. Second, the distributions of subjective prospects in the two conditions overlapped considerably (Figure 2), and subjective prospects were only weakly correlated with behavioral intentions, which likely diluted any between-condition difference in those intentions. Finally, more participants in the positive prospects condition were excluded for failing the comprehension checks, raising the possibility that the two groups differed in attention.

Figure 2: Distribution of subjective prospects in the negative and positive prospects conditions of Study 1 (kernel density estimates). Vertical lines mark the condition means; the bracket shows the Welch t test of the manipulation check. Higher scores indicate more negative prospects.

We conducted Study 2 to test whether the correlations of negative subjective prospects with purchase intention and private information-sharing intention would replicate in a new context. Because the behavioral items were developed for Study 1, Study 2 also examined the replicability of the three-factor structure.

3. Study 2: A Preregistered Conceptual Replication with Different Products

Building on Study 1, where subjective prospects correlated significantly with both purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, Study 2 served as a preregistered conceptual replication using two other everyday essentials, toilet paper and laundry detergent (OSF preregistration). The survey was conducted in June 2026, during the 2026 Strait of Hormuz oil supply crisis. Because a real crisis was under way, we did not manipulate subjective prospects; instead, we measured them and assessed the correlation between subjective prospects and consumers’ behavioral intentions in this crisis. In May 2026, newspaper reports and manufacturer announcements named both toilet paper and laundry detergent among the everyday essentials likely to be affected by the oil shock (Daio Paper Corporation, 2026; “Gen’yu・Nafusa Busoku,” 2026), but neither had yet run short, so participants responded to a possible shortage rather than to one they were already experiencing.

The preregistered hypotheses were as follows.

  • H1. The twelve behavioral items reproduce the three-factor structure of Study 1, comprising purchase intention, private information-sharing intention, and public information-sharing intention.
  • H2a. Negative subjective prospects about the supply of the target product are positively associated with purchase intention.
  • H2b. Negative subjective prospects are positively associated with private information-sharing intention.
  • H3. Subjective prospects are not associated with public information-sharing intention.

The preregistration states H2a, H2b, and H3 in terms of perceived stability. For consistency with Study 1, we report them using the reversed score, subjective prospects (where higher values indicate more negative prospects), so that H2a and H2b predict positive associations. Product type was included as a between-participants factor to assess generalizability, and no difference between the two products was hypothesized.

3.1. Method

We recruited Japanese adults aged 30 to 60, as preregistered, through Cross Marketing Inc. on June 10–11, 2026, and analyzed 536 of 1,028 responses after the preregistered exclusions (53.7% men; age M = 44.66, SD = 8.71; 257 toilet paper, 279 laundry detergent; exclusions in Appendix 6.3.1). The planned sample of 500 gave power of .80 to detect r = .13 (significance level \(\alpha\) = .05, two-tailed test), slightly smaller than the smallest relevant correlation in Study 1. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Graduate School of Humanities and Sociology, University of Tokyo (UTSP-25047).

Participants were randomly assigned to either the toilet paper or the laundry detergent condition and first read a short description of the oil supply crisis. They then rated their subjective prospects for the supply of the assigned product and responded to the same direct and indirect observation contexts as in Study 1, with presentation order counterbalanced. Each context was illustrated with an AI-generated image of the target product, and participants were explicitly told that the images were generated using AI (Figure 3). Six attention checks were embedded in the survey (Appendix 6.3.1).

Figure 3: Pictures shown in the direct observation context (left) and the indirect observation context (right) of Study 2, for toilet paper (top) and laundry detergent (bottom). All pictures were generated using AI, and participants were told so.

Study materials are available on the Open Science Framework. [NOTE: make the OSF registration and materials public before final submission; the current URL is view-only.]

3.1.1. Measures

Subjective Prospects. Participants’ subjective prospects for the supply of the assigned product were measured with three 5-point scale items adapted from Study 1. These asked whether its supply would become unstable, whether the participant could obtain it as usual, and whether it would sell out in stores. Items were coded so that higher values indicate more negative prospects and then aggregated (Cronbach’s \(\alpha\) = .72).

Purchase Intention and Information-sharing Intention. Purchase intention (three items per context) and information-sharing intention (two private sharing items and one public sharing item per context) were measured on the same 5-point scale (1 = definitely not to 5 = definitely) as in Study 1, except that the household stock levels in the purchase items were reworded to suit the target products (Table 5).

3.2. Results

3.2.1. Behavioral variables

To test H1, we fitted the preregistered confirmatory factor analysis (robust maximum likelihood using the lavaan package of R; R Core Team, 2026; Rosseel, 2012). The tested model imposed twelve behavioral items on three independent factors: purchase intention (six items), private information-sharing intention (four items), and public information-sharing intention (two items). We used the following criteria: CFI and TLI \(\ge\) .90, RMSEA and SRMR \(\le\) .08.

The model did not fit the data well (\(\chi^2\)[54] = 1103.70, p < .001, CFI = .715, TLI = .652, RMSEA = .202, SRMR = .214), and the preregistered fallback allowing an oblique factor structure also failed to achieve the preregistered criteria (\(\chi^2\)[51] = 884.59, p < .001, CFI = .768, TLI = .699, RMSEA = .188, SRMR = .089). H1 was therefore not supported by the CFA. Following the next preregistered fallback, we checked the internal consistency of the three item groups; all three were acceptable (\(\alpha\) = .88 for purchase intention, .87 for private information-sharing intention, and .86 for public information-sharing intention; r = .75 between the two public information-sharing items), so we used their item means to test H2a, H2b and H3.

An exploratory factor analysis (minimum residual extraction with varimax rotation, as in Study 1) recovered the three factors observed in Study 1 (Table 2). Three eigenvalues exceeded 1 (5.03, 2.40 and 1.21; the fourth was 0.83), and the three factors explained 63.4% of the total variance. Every item loaded highest on its preregistered factor, and the promax solution gave the same pattern (Appendix 6.3.2).

3.2.2. Subjective prospects and behavioral intentions

We tested H2a, H2b and H3 by computing Pearson’s product-moment correlations between subjective prospects and behavioral intention scores in the pooled sample (Table 3). The subjective prospects \(\times\) purchase intention correlation was significant (r[534] = .18, 95% CI [.09, .26], p < .001), supporting H2a, and the subjective prospects \(\times\) private information-sharing intention correlation was also significant (r[534] = .20, 95% CI [.11, .28], p < .001), supporting H2b. Contrary to H3, the subjective prospects \(\times\) public information-sharing intention correlation was also significant (r[534] = .19, 95% CI [.10, .27], p < .001). These associations held for both commodities when each commodity was analyzed separately (Appendix 6.3.3).

3.3. Discussion

Across the two studies, consumers with more negative subjective prospects responded to shortage information with higher purchase intention and higher private information-sharing intention, as hypothesized, with correlations of about .2 in both studies (Table 3 and Figure 4). Responses in different contexts (i.e., direct and indirect observation) loaded on the same factor as long as their behavioral outputs were the same (purchase vs. privately sharing information vs. publicly sharing information). Although CFA failed to support this three-factor structure with strict criteria, EFA replicated it. Moreover, in both Studies 1 and 2, negative prospects for supply were positively associated with purchase intention and private information-sharing intention.

In Study 2, the preregistered CFA did not support the hypothesized three-factor structure, whereas EFA recovered the same three factors, with every factor loaded by the exact same items as in Study 1. In retrospect, the preregistered CFA criteria may have been too strict for a model that was not theoretically derived and was instead used to organize different behavioral responses across contexts empirically.

Across both studies, participants encountered shortage information in a scenario featuring either a nearly empty shelf or a social media post and reported how they would respond. Subjective prospects, which indicate how strongly a consumer perceives a crisis, were positively associated with these responses, though the associations were small. Because such correlations describe only individual responses and cannot show how consumers’ actions interact over time, the next section uses an agent-based simulation to examine whether behavioral rules qualitatively grounded in these findings can accelerate stock depletion through purchases and private sharing.

4. Study 3: An Agent-Based Simulation of Shortage Information on a Network of Close Relationships

In Studies 1 and 2, negative subjective prospects about future supply were consistently associated with higher purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, whereas public information-sharing intention remained rare and inconsistently linked to subjective prospects. However, these effects were small. The correlations were around r = .20, a small-to-medium effect by Cohen’s (1988) benchmarks. This is consistent with earlier findings that most consumers respond to crises with modest rather than extreme changes in buying (Bentall et al., 2021; Hori & Iwamoto, 2014; O’Connell et al., 2021). Yet real shortages often involve severe depletion that spreads widely within a short period (Iizuka et al., 2022; Upton & Nuttall, 2014; Wei et al., 2011). Because survey data capture individual intentions at a single point in time, they cannot show how small individual shifts combine into a market-wide shortage. Study 3 therefore takes the micro-macro approach set out in the introduction (Schelling, 1978; Yamagishi, 1992). In an agent-based simulation, each purchase depletes a local retailer, and each act of sharing passes shortage information to close others, so the consequences of individual behavior feed back into the conditions that other consumers face. The micro-level behavioral rules are empirically grounded in Studies 1 and 2 at the qualitative level. Consumers shift their purchase probability in a modest, graded way, buy a single unit, share shortage information privately rather than broadcasting it, and share secondhand information somewhat less often than firsthand information. The simulation does not calibrate exact probability parameters to the survey data. Instead, it varies the two behavioral tendencies systematically to test whether small increases in purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, interacting with fixed local retailer stock and a small-world social network of mostly local ties and a few long-range ties, are enough to produce rapid, widespread depletion. The results show that market-wide depletion can occur without dramatic changes in individual behavior.

4.1. Model

4.1.1. Overview

The model represents a retail market during a short shortage window of one to two weeks, as in Japan’s 2020 toilet-paper shortage (Iizuka et al., 2022; Japan Household Paper Industry Association, 2020a) and the 2012 United Kingdom fuel shortage, which largely subsided within two weeks (Upton & Nuttall, 2014). Rather than modeling supply-side dynamics, the model takes a minimal approach by holding retailer stock fixed without restocking, isolating whether demand-side behavior alone can produce widespread stock-outs. In real crises, shopping and supply are geographically local. Survey evidence from the 2020 Japanese toilet-paper shortage shows that consumers’ store choices remained an extension of their everyday shopping habits, concentrating at familiar neighborhood stores where many failed to obtain stock once shelves emptied (Sekiguchi et al., 2022). To represent this local structure, the model divides the market into districts, each with a local retailer holding fixed stock, where consumers visit their own district first and search nearby districts only if their local retailer is empty (Figures 5b and 5c). Because total market supply is fixed in the model, the primary dependent variable is depletion time, defined as how quickly the entire stock runs out. Depletion time thus links individual behavioral shifts to the risk of a market-wide shortage. When changes in consumer behavior raise aggregate demand, stock depletes faster.

On the demand side, the model represents how individual consumers notice, react to, and share information about shortages during a crisis. Household scanner studies of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake in Japan (Hori & Iwamoto, 2014) and the early 2020 COVID-19 shortage in the United Kingdom (O’Connell et al., 2021) show that aggregate demand spikes were driven mainly by more households choosing to buy rather than by extreme hoarding. Accordingly, each consumer in the model purchases at most a single unit of goods during the shortage window. In Studies 1 and 2, consumers with more negative subjective prospects reported higher purchase intention when encountering shortage information and higher private information-sharing intention with close others. To represent these two responses conceptually, receiving shortage information increases a consumer’s purchase probability, and consumers can share shortage information with close others either after encountering an empty retailer directly or after receiving shortage information indirectly (Figure 6). By contrast, because public information-sharing intention was rare and inconsistently linked to subjective prospects across Studies 1 and 2 (Table 3; Figure 4), the model leaves out market-wide broadcasting and focuses on purchasing and private information sharing as the two consumer behaviors.

These design choices respond to the limits of prior models identified in the introduction. The closest prior model, by Upton and Nuttall (2014), also links local stockouts to shortage information passed across a small-world network, but the present model differs in three respects. First, drivers in their model make an abrupt binary switch into panic, whereas consumers in the present model only shift their per-step purchase probability within a modest range and buy at most a single unit. Second, their mechanism depends on fuel tanks and repeated refueling, whereas the present model has no product-specific mechanics and represents a single purchase of an everyday essential during a short shortage window. Third, their behavioral and communication rules are assumed, whereas the present rules are empirically grounded in Studies 1 and 2. Purchase and private sharing both rise with shortage information, public broadcasting is left out, and secondhand sharing is set below firsthand sharing.

Figure 5: Conceptual diagram of the network simulation model (scaled-down illustration). (a) The consumer network at four rewiring probabilities (\(p^{\text{RW}}\) = 0%, 0.5%, 2%, and 10%). Dashed lines represent long-range ties created by rewiring. (b) One network at a 2% rewiring probability. Consumers are placed on a ring of 25 districts, numbered 0 to 24 clockwise from the top. Each district has one retailer that holds fixed initial stock with no restocking, except for the retailer in district 0, which starts with zero stock. Each consumer has 10 local ties (5 per side) to the nearest consumers on both sides of the ring, and rewiring replaces local ties with long-range ties to randomly chosen consumers. (c) The focal consumer marked in (b). The consumer shops first at the retailer in their own district, then at the retailers in the two neighboring districts in random order, and then at the retailers in the two second-order neighboring districts in random order. For display, the number of consumers and ties is reduced: each district shows 4 of its 100 consumers; tie counts in (a) are in proportion to the model; (b) shows 2 of the 5 local ties on each side; and (c) is schematic and shows 3 on each side.

Figure 6: Stages of one simulation step. In Stage 2, consumers decide to share secondhand shortage information with probability \(p^{\text{S2}} = 0.8 \times p^{\text{S1}}\). In Stage 3, consumers decide to attempt a purchase with probability \(p_{i,t}^{\text{BUY}}\), which increases with the number of network neighbors currently sharing (\(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}}\); Figure 7). Each consumer makes this decision only once; after an unsuccessful attempt, the consumer continues searching nearby retailers without making a new decision. In Stage 4, consumers decide to share firsthand shortage information with probability \(p^{\text{S1}}\). Each run ends when all stock is depleted or after 150 steps.

Finally, while shopping is physically constrained to a consumer’s local neighborhood, private communication with close others need not be. Close others such as family members and close friends may live outside the neighborhood and be contacted by phone or private messaging. To represent this possibility, consumers are connected in a small-world network (Watts & Strogatz, 1998) consisting mostly of local ties within the same or nearby districts alongside a small proportion of long-range ties across distant districts (Figures 5a and 5b). Because even a few long-range ties allow shortage information to travel across otherwise separate districts, the simulation also varies the proportion of long-range ties to examine how network structure interacts with consumer behavior to affect depletion time.

4.1.2. Model Details

Population and network. The population consisting of consumers and retailers is initialized with \(N = 2,500\) homogeneous consumers distributed evenly across \(D = 25\) districts on a circular ring (100 residents per district; Figure 5b; Table 4). Each consumer initially has 10 network neighbors who are the five nearest consumers on each side on the ring (\(k = 10\)). Most of the initial neighbors reside in the same district as the focal consumer. Each edge in the ring network is rewired to a randomly chosen consumer with probability \(p^{\text{RW}}\) to transform the regular ring lattice to a small-world network (Figure 5a).

There are 25 retailers in the population, one in each district. At the outset (step 0), all retailers except one hold 50 units of non-replenished goods. One retailer located in district 0 holds no goods at step 0 to seed a single local shortage. Consequently, there are initially 1,200 units of the goods across the population. As there are more consumers (2,500) than units of the goods (1,200), market-wide depletion eventually occurs.

Consumer actions. In the model, consumers take at most three actions by the end of a simulation run: to purchase a single unit of goods, to share firsthand information with network neighbors (i.e., other consumers connected with the focal consumer), and to share secondhand information with network neighbors.

First, each consumer purchases at most one unit of goods from one of five nearby retailers during a simulation run. Because this simulation models consumer behavior within a period short enough that retailers cannot restock, each consumer needs only a single unit of goods (i.e., the model excludes hoarding). Consumers visit retailers in the following order until they can make a purchase: the retailer in their own district, one of the randomly selected retailers in the two neighboring districts, the retailer in the remaining neighboring district, one of the randomly selected retailers in the two second-order neighboring districts, and the retailer in the remaining second-order neighboring district (Figure 5c). If more consumers visit a retailer in a step than it has units remaining, the retailer sells those units to randomly selected consumers, and the unselected consumers visit the next retailer on their route in the following step. Before purchasing one unit of goods, consumer \(i\) decides whether to attempt a purchase at step \(t\) with probability \(p_{i,t}^{\text{BUY}}\). When consumer \(i\) receives no shortage information from their network neighbors at step \(t\) (\(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} = 0\)), they attempt a purchase with probability .01 (\(p_{0} = .01\)). When consumer \(i\) receives shortage information from \(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}}\) network neighbors (\(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} > 0\)), consumer \(i\)’s purchase probability \(p_{i,t}^{\text{BUY}}\) increases following the sigmoid function defined below:

\begin{equation*} p_{i,t}^{\text{BUY}} = \begin{cases} p_{0}, & n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} = 0,\\ p_{0} + \dfrac{p_{\max} - p_{0}}{1 + e^{-g (n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} - m)}}, & n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} > 0, \end{cases} \end{equation*}

where \(p_{0}\) is the baseline purchase probability (set to .01 in this simulation), \(p_{\max}\) is the maximum purchase probability (set to .10), \(g\) is the steepness of the sigmoid function (set to 20), and \(m\) is the reaction midpoint, which is a function of reaction sensitivity \(s \in [0, 1]\): \(m = 0.5 + k(1 - s)\) (Figure 7). For example, when consumers are maximally sensitive to shortage information (i.e., \(s = 1\)), \(m\) is 0.5, and even a single source of shortage information (\(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} = 1\)) makes \(p_{i,t}^{\text{BUY}} \approx p_{\max}\). When consumers are minimally sensitive (i.e., \(s = 0\)), \(m\) is \(k + 0.5 = 10.5\), and even shortage information from 10 network neighbors (\(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} = 10\)) yields \(p_{i,t}^{\text{BUY}} \approx p_{0}\); only consumers who gain more than 10 network neighbors through rewiring can exceed the reaction midpoint (Appendix 6.4.2). We set the steepness to \(g = 20\) so that the reaction is step-like. Below the reaction midpoint, purchase probability stays near \(p_{0}\), and above it, purchase probability stays near \(p_{\max}\). This choice keeps the results easy to interpret, because reaction sensitivity then sets a single threshold number of sharing neighbors. The step-like shape does not represent a switch into panic or hoarding. It only changes the per-step probability of attempting to buy a single unit, within a modest range from .01 to .10. With smoother reaction curves (\(g = 1\) and \(g = 2\)), the results were almost the same (Appendix 6.4.2).

Figure 7: Purchase probability per step by the number of network neighbors sharing shortage information, at three levels of reaction sensitivity \(s\). Dots mark integer counts, and the smooth line shows the sigmoid. With zero network neighbors sharing shortage information, purchase probability is fixed at the baseline \(p_{0}\); with one or more, it follows the sigmoid. The dashed vertical line marks the average number of network neighbors, \(k = 10\), which remains constant across rewiring levels; counts above 10 occur only after rewiring. In all panels, \(p_{0} = .01\), \(p_{\max} = .10\), and \(g = 20\).

Second, each consumer has at most one opportunity to share firsthand shortage information during a simulation run. When consumer \(i\) attempts a purchase and finds a retailer empty, they observe the shortage themselves. At their first such observation, consumer \(i\) starts sharing shortage information with probability \(p^{\text{S1}}\), which is varied in the simulation. A consumer who shares shortage information broadcasts it to all of their network neighbors, starting at the next step and lasting 10 steps, and counts as one source in each neighbor’s \(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}}\).

Third, each consumer has at most one opportunity to share secondhand shortage information during a simulation run. When consumer \(i\) receives shortage information from at least one network neighbor (\(n_{i,t}^{\text{INFO}} > 0\)) and has not yet attempted a purchase, they start sharing shortage information in the same manner with probability \(p^{\text{S2}} = 0.8 \times p^{\text{S1}}\). This fixed fraction is based on Studies 1 and 2, in which sharing after indirect observation was slightly lower than sharing after direct observation (Appendices 6.2.8 and 6.3.4).

The primary dependent variable is depletion time \(T\), defined as the number of steps that the population of consumers takes to purchase the entire stocks (up to a ceiling of 150 steps). This simulation implemented 50 runs with random seeds for the same parameter set and averaged the 50 \(T\)s.

4.2. Results and Discussion

To establish the range of possible depletion times, we first set the firsthand information sharing probability to zero (\(p^{\text{S1}} = 0\)) so that every consumer had the same constant purchase probability, and varied this probability from .01 to .10 in steps of .005, each end corresponding to \(p_{0}\) and \(p_{\max}\), respectively. Depletion time fell steadily as purchase probability increased (Figure 8). The market ran out of stock after 74.3 steps (mean of 50 runs) when purchase probability was set to .01, which serves as the slowest reference point for this simulation. When purchase probability was set to .10, the market ran out of stock after 8.4 steps (the fastest reference point). We use these reference points to interpret all later results because shortage information affects the market only through changes in consumers’ purchase probability. Depletion time near the slowest reference point means that the socially shared information barely increases the risk of market-wide depletion, whereas the one near the fastest reference point means that it increases the risk to the highest end.

Figure 8: Depletion time (steps) at a constant purchase probability per step, with no information sharing (\(p^{\text{S1}} = 0\)). Purchase probability ranges from .01 (\(p_{0}\)) to .10 (\(p_{\max}\)) in steps of .005. Each point shows the mean of 50 runs, and the shaded band shows one standard deviation above and below the mean. Dashed lines mark the slowest (74.3 steps) and fastest (8.4 steps) reference points.

Next, we ran a set of simulations varying reaction sensitivity (\(s\) from 0 to 1 with an increment of 0.05), firsthand information sharing probability (\(p^{\text{S1}}\) from 0 to 1 with an increment of 0.05), and rewiring probability (12 levels from 0% to 10%; Table 4). Each combination of the three parameters was repeated 50 times. Figure 9 shows four rewiring probabilities (0%, 0.5%, 2%, and 10%). When consumers were connected only with physical neighbors (\(p^{\text{RW}} = 0\)), depletion time remained near the slowest reference point across almost all combinations of \(s\) and \(p^{\text{S1}}\) (Figure 9a). Depletion time was only slightly shorter (at the upper-right corner, 13% faster than the slowest reference point) even when both reaction sensitivity and firsthand information sharing probability were near their maximum.

However, even a small change in rewiring probability had a large effect on depletion time, especially when both reaction sensitivity and firsthand information sharing probability increased. In small-world networks (Figures 9b--9d), the two behavioral parameters together produced a shift from slowest to fastest depletion time. In each panel, reaction sensitivity increases upward and firsthand information sharing probability increases to the right. Even at a small rewiring probability (0.5% or \(p^{\text{RW}} = .005\)), a region of fast depletion emerged in the upper right (at the upper-right corner, 58% faster than the slowest reference point). This tendency was amplified when rewiring probability increased to 2% (and to 10%). The presence of edges connecting physically distant districts on the ring lattice allowed the shortage information to reach distant districts, which in turn increased purchase probability in physically diverse districts. Therefore, local depletion occurred simultaneously in distant districts. It is noteworthy that, when combined, reaction sensitivity and firsthand information sharing probability had a major effect on depletion time. Thus, the empirical correlations (significant positive correlations of negative prospects with purchase intention and information-sharing intention) may substantially shorten depletion time because these correlations together shift consumer behavior toward the upper-right region.

Figure 9: Mean depletion time (steps) across reaction sensitivity (\(s\)) and firsthand information sharing probability (\(p^{\text{S1}}\)) at four rewiring probabilities: (a) \(p^{\text{RW}} = 0\), (b) \(p^{\text{RW}} = .005\), (c) \(p^{\text{RW}} = .02\), and (d) \(p^{\text{RW}} = .10\). Reaction sensitivity increases upward and firsthand information sharing probability increases to the right. Each cell shows the mean of 50 runs; cells are shown in steps of .1. Outlined cells A–F mark the six parameter pairs plotted in Figure 10. The full set of rewiring probabilities is shown in Appendix 6.4.1.

To illustrate how individual behavioral combinations behaved across the full range of rewiring probabilities, Figure 10 plots mean depletion time as a function of rewiring probability (\(p^{\text{RW}}\), starting from 0%) for six representative parameter pairs, marked A–F in Figure 9: the four extreme corner regimes, A (low sensitivity–low sharing; \(s = .1\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .1\)), B (high sensitivity–low sharing; \(s = 1\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .1\)), C (low sensitivity–high sharing; \(s = .1\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = 1\)), and D (high sensitivity–high sharing; \(s = 1\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = 1\)), and two closely spaced parameter pairs located on either side of the boundary, E (\(s = .6\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .6\)) and F (\(s = .7\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .7\)). At \(p^{\text{RW}} = 0\), five of the six pairs remained near the slowest reference point; only the high–high pair was somewhat faster. As rewiring increased, the low–low and high-sensitivity–low-sharing pairs remained near the slowest reference point, the low-sensitivity–high-sharing pair became only slightly faster, and the high–high pair fell sharply by 1% rewiring before approaching the fastest reference point at high rewiring. Once rewiring was present, a small increase in both behavioral parameters from the pair just below the boundary (E) to the pair just above it (F) produced a large drop in depletion time, showing that a small change in behavior could have a large effect. Without rewiring, the two near-boundary lines were almost together, but with rewiring they separated widely, and the width of the gap between them in Figure 10 showed how much the risk of market-wide depletion increased.

Figure 10: Mean depletion time (steps) across rewiring probability (\(p^{\text{RW}}\), starting from 0%) for four corner regimes (low–low, high–low, low–high, high–high) and two closely spaced combinations straddling the boundary. Each point is the mean of 50 matched runs.

Together, the heatmaps (Figure 9) and the line plot (Figure 10) show the same pattern. When consumers make a purchase near home but share shortage information with distant network partners, the possibility of market-wide depletion sharply increases. Figure 10 shows that such a sharp increase is unlikely if either purchase intention or information-sharing intention stays low. Although the effects on purchase intention and private information-sharing intention in Studies 1 and 2 were small, both of them were correlated with negative prospects. When these parameters increased together, market-wide depletion became more likely. Thus, this simulation showed that the empirical pattern of correlations, each of which had a small effect independently, may have larger joint effects on the market.

5. General Discussion

This thesis addressed the micro-macro gap in panic buying research, asking how everyday essentials can disappear from retail shelves across a market within days when individual consumers make only modest adjustments. Across two empirical studies and an agent-based simulation, the findings link individual responses to shortage information with market-wide stock depletion. Studies 1 and 2 showed that more negative subjective prospects are reliably, but modestly, associated with stronger purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, whereas public information-sharing intention remains rare. Study 3 then showed that, when micro-level behavioral rules qualitatively grounded in these tendencies operate across local retailers and a small-world network of close relationships, rapid stock depletion can emerge without panicking consumers, heavy stockpiling, or public broadcasting.

5.1. Interpreting the Individual-Level Findings

Taken together, Studies 1 and 2 point to a consistent psychological pattern across two non-COVID crisis contexts and three everyday essentials (rice, toilet paper, and laundry detergent). First, individual differences linked to subjective prospects were stable in direction and consistently small, with correlations of r = .18 to .20 accounting for roughly 3% to 4% of the variance in purchase intention and private information-sharing intention (Table 3). In Study 1, newspaper excerpts shifted subjective prospects substantially without moving purchase intention, and in Study 2, general crisis concern added to intentions without amplifying the slope of subjective prospects (Appendix 6.3.3). These modest associations align closely with empirical household scanner records and nationally representative surveys, which find little evidence for widespread extreme hoarding and show instead that aggregate demand spikes are driven primarily by a larger share of households buying modestly within the same window (Bentall et al., 2021; Hori & Iwamoto, 2014; O’Connell et al., 2021).

Second, the factor structure of behavioral responses proved more informative than the size of any single correlation. In both studies, exploratory factor analyses separated responses by behavioral channel (purchase intention, private information-sharing intention, and public information-sharing intention) rather than by whether shortage information was encountered directly at a nearly empty shelf or indirectly on social media. Private information-sharing intention occupied a central position, correlating moderately with purchase intention and rising consistently with more negative subjective prospects. Public information-sharing intention, by contrast, remained very low in both studies (M = 1.71 in Study 1 and M = 1.67 in Study 2 on a 5-point scale; Table 3) and was unrelated to purchase intention.

Third, Study 2 did not support preregistered Hypothesis 3, which predicted no association between subjective prospects and public information-sharing intention. Unlike in Study 1 (r = .05), more negative subjective prospects were positively associated with public information-sharing intention in Study 2 (r = .19). One plausible reason is the difference in crisis timing. Study 1 took place months after the peak of the 2024–2025 rice shortage, whereas Study 2 took place during the unfolding 2026 Strait of Hormuz oil supply crisis, when media attention was active and no shortage had yet materialized. Under active uncertainty, pessimistic consumers may become slightly more willing to post or repost publicly. Even so, because mean public information-sharing intention remained near the floor of the scale, this association describes a behavior that few participants reported they would perform. The empirical pattern therefore points toward private sharing among family, friends, and acquaintances, rather than public broadcasting to strangers, as the primary everyday channel through which consumers pass along shortage information.

5.2. Bridging the Micro-Macro Gap and Positioning Against Prior Models

The central contribution of this thesis is showing how these modest micro-level tendencies can produce rapid market-wide stock depletion when coupled with local retail inventory. In the framework of micro-macro social psychology (Schelling, 1978; Yamagishi, 1992), individual purchases alter objective reality by emptying local shelves, while private sharing alters social reality by passing shortage information to close contacts before they visit a store. Study 3 implemented this feedback loop using behavioral rules qualitatively grounded in Studies 1 and 2. Consumers adjusted their per-step purchase probability within a modest bounded range (.01 to .10), bought at most a single unit, shared shortage information privately rather than broadcasting it publicly, and shared secondhand information slightly less often than firsthand information.

The simulation results demonstrate two properties that single-level surveys cannot detect. First, reaction sensitivity and private sharing act synergistically once even a small fraction of close relationships reaches other districts (Figures 9 and 10). At 1% rewiring (\(p^{\text{RW}} = .01\)), raising reaction sensitivity alone from the low-low corner (cell A; \(s = .10\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .10\); 74.3 steps) to the high-sensitivity corner (cell B; \(s = 1\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .10\)) sped stock depletion by only 1.1%, and raising private sharing alone (cell C; \(s = .10\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = 1\)) sped depletion by only 2.1%. Raising both together (cell D; \(s = 1\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = 1\); 22.9 steps) sped depletion by 69.2% relative to the slowest reference point, far exceeding the sum of the two separate effects (compared with 13.4% at 0% rewiring and 58.0% at 0.5% rewiring). Second, rapid acceleration does not require extreme parameter corners. Once long-range ties are present, a modest joint shift of .10 in both parameters across the transition boundary, from cell E (\(s = .60\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .60\)) to cell F (\(s = .70\), \(p^{\text{S1}} = .70\)), shortened depletion time by 29.1% at 1% rewiring (67.9 to 48.1 steps), 45.8% at 2% rewiring (59.9 to 32.4 steps), and 58.7% at 10% rewiring (46.2 to 19.1 steps), whereas the same shift shortened depletion time by only 2.8% without rewiring (0%). Conversely, when both tendencies stayed below the boundary, depletion remained near the slowest reference point across all rewiring levels. This explains why panic buying remains rare in normal times even though private communication channels are always available.

This mechanism also clarifies how a crisis can trigger a market-wide shortage without transforming consumers into panicked hoarders. Consistent with the additive effect of crisis concern observed in Study 2 (Appendix 6.3.3), common external shocks such as mass media reports or official crisis warnings can nudge many consumers slightly in the same direction at the same time (Fukutomi, 2024; Keane & Neal, 2021). When a shared shock slightly raises both purchase readiness and willingness to warn close contacts, it moves the population jointly toward the nonlinear boundary where local stockouts and private sharing reinforce one another across districts. Rapid market-wide stock depletion can therefore arise without extreme individual overreaction and without public broadcasting on social media.

Positioned against the prior literature reviewed in the Introduction, these findings address all three forms of the micro-macro gap. First, unlike micro-level studies that treat shortage information as an external input, Study 3 explicitly models how purchases and private sharing generate the shortage information that other consumers subsequently face. Second, in contrast to macro-level and formal models that rely on extreme or assumed individual rules, our results show that rapid stock depletion requires neither abrupt panic switches nor heavy stockpiling. For example, Miyashita et al. (2025) modeled Japan’s 2020 toilet-paper shortage on an online social network using assumed parameters, selfish-buying switches, and no physical stores. Economic equilibrium models by Noda and Teramoto (2024) and Klumpp and Su (2025) derive shortage spirals from fully rational, forward-looking consumers who anticipate higher shopping costs or coordinate on heavy stockpiling up to storage limits after an external shock, without a private-sharing network or crisis consumer data. Study 3 shows that none of these strong cognitive or behavioral assumptions is necessary for rapid stock depletion.

Third, the present thesis extends the two closest micro-macro agent-based models and offers a complementary mechanism to aggregate social media accounts. Upton and Nuttall (2014) captured local stockout feedback on a small-world network for UK fuel panics, but they assumed all behavioral and communication parameters without consumer survey data, relied on a binary panic switch, and depended on fuel-tank mechanics and repeated refueling. Dulam et al. (2021a, 2021b) combined survey data with local retail stores, but they modeled fixed personal and household traits, coded roughly a third of households as heavy stockpilers from the outset, and entered media reports and rumors as external inputs rather than endogenous private sharing. By qualitatively grounding both buying and private sharing in crisis survey data while restricting purchases to a single unit and bounded probability shifts, Study 3 removes binary panic switches, preset heavy stockpilers, and product-specific mechanics. Finally, compared with Iizuka et al. (2022), who inferred pluralistic ignorance from regressions of daily supermarket sales on public Twitter views while omitting store stockouts and household saturation, our framework offers a concrete physical and interpersonal alternative. Even when consumers rarely broadcast publicly and do not believe extreme rumors, local retail stockouts and private sharing among close contacts can drive a rapid surge in buying and its subsequent decline once shelves empty and households complete their purchases. In addition, Studies 1 and 2 contribute empirical evidence from two non-COVID crises in Japan to a literature heavily concentrated on COVID-19 (Appendix 6.5).

5.3. Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations qualify these conclusions and point directly to future work. First, the simulation is qualitatively grounded in the behavioral tendencies observed in Studies 1 and 2, not quantitatively calibrated to them. Exact probability parameters (\(p_{0}\), \(p_{\max}\), \(g\), \(s\), and \(p^{\text{S1}}\)) were chosen to explore model behavior rather than estimated from survey responses, and this thesis does not establish a direct quantitative mapping from the observed correlations (r = .18 to .20) to specific shifts in \((s, p^{\text{S1}})\). In particular, rapid depletion in the simulation emerged mainly in the upper-right region (\(s\) and \(p^{\text{S1}}\) around .60 or higher). The simulation therefore establishes theoretical sufficiency under qualitatively grounded rules (Epstein, 1999) rather than predicting the exact threshold of a specific real-world shortage.

Second, several structural simplifications in Study 3 bound its generalizability. Setting sigmoid steepness to \(g = 20\) creates a step-like reaction curve around the midpoint number of sharing neighbors. Although this step operates only within a modest per-step probability band (.01 to .10) for a single unit rather than representing panic or hoarding, and robustness checks with smoother curves (\(g = 1\) and \(g = 2\)) produced almost the same depletion patterns (Appendix 6.4.2), real consumers may update their behavior more gradually. Moreover, total initial stock (1,200 units) was fixed below the population size (2,500 consumers) with no restocking, so market-wide depletion was guaranteed by design and depletion speed served as the outcome. Real retail systems restock continuously, and shortages occur when temporary demand surges outpace replenishment. The model also assumed homogeneous consumers on a static network, excluded public sharing, and restricted each consumer to a single unit. Restricting purchases to one unit isolates the participation channel emphasized by scanner studies, but it excludes quantity effects from households that buy extra units even without extreme hoarding. Omitting public sharing tested whether private sharing alone suffices, yet Study 2’s positive correlation for public sharing suggests that even a small active minority posting publicly could interact with private sharing.

Third, the empirical studies carry methodological and contextual limitations. Both studies relied on online panels and measured self-reported intentions in hypothetical scenarios with AI-generated images rather than observed purchases or actual messages. Because the key associations are cross-sectional, they do not establish that negative subjective prospects causally increase buying or sharing, especially since the Study 1 news manipulation moved subjective prospects strongly without altering purchase intention. Furthermore, the empirical contexts did not match pure demand-driven shortages with intact physical supply. Study 1 followed the 2024–2025 Reiwa rice shortage, which involved a real supply shortfall caused by extreme weather alongside higher demand, whereas Study 2 was conducted during the 2026 Strait of Hormuz oil supply crisis before any actual shortage of toilet paper or laundry detergent had occurred.

Fourth, sample exclusions and measurement properties warrant caution. Substantial proportions of responses were excluded for failing comprehension or attention checks, 46% of consenting responses in Study 1 (246 of 530; Table 6) and 41% of eligible responses in Study 2, where eligible refers to consenting adults aged 30 to 60 who took at least 60 seconds (365 of 901; Table 13). The analyzed samples therefore overrepresent attentive respondents. In Study 1, comprehension checks excluded more participants in the positive prospects condition than in the negative prospects condition, weakening causal comparisons between conditions. In Study 2, the preregistered confirmatory factor analysis did not meet its fit criteria even though exploratory factor analysis replicated the exact three-factor loading pattern from Study 1, indicating that the three intention factors are correlated rather than strictly orthogonal, and preregistered Hypothesis 3 was not supported (r = .19).

Four steps would directly connect these empirical and modeling strands in future research. First, replacing homogeneous agents with heterogeneous consumers whose purchase readiness and sharing propensities follow empirical survey distributions, including a small tail of active public sharers, would test how population diversity shifts the transition boundary. Second, directly measuring the share of close contacts who live and shop in other retail districts would empirically anchor the rewiring parameter that proved decisive in the simulation. Third, adding retail restocking dynamics and modest multi-unit purchase decisions would allow shortages to emerge and subside endogenously rather than guaranteeing depletion. Fourth, pairing household scanner records with behavioral messaging or mobility data during unfolding crises would test whether the modest shifts observed in survey intentions translate into actual purchasing and private sharing in the field.

5.4. Conclusion

Consumers respond to shortage information in modest and stable ways, reporting slightly stronger purchase intention and private information-sharing intention when their subjective prospects worsen while rarely broadcasting shortages publicly. Yet when local retail stockouts and private sharing among close relationships feed back into one another across a small-world social network, those modest individual tendencies are enough to accelerate market-wide stock depletion without panicking consumers, heavy stockpiling, or public broadcasts. Large-scale panic buying can therefore emerge as an unintended macro-level consequence of ordinary, slightly shifted consumer behavior.
