6.2. Study 1

6.2.1. Newspaper Article Stimuli

Participants read two newspaper excerpts in their assigned news condition. The following summaries and comprehension items are translated from the Japanese questionnaire. Each article was followed by two questions with two response options. Correct answers are identified below. The names of the researchers quoted in the two Asahi articles were anonymized in the questionnaire.

6.2.1.1. Negative condition

The first article, “New rice prices rise despite increased production,” appeared in Nihon Keizai Shimbun on October 18, 2025 (morning edition, p. 5). The excerpt described persistent risks to rice supply. Extreme heat and other weather damage made harvest volumes harder to predict, while the aging agricultural workforce weakened the production base.

  1. According to the article, why has it become harder to predict rice harvest volumes? Options were (a) damage from insects and wild animals and (b) weather damage such as extreme heat. Correct answer was (b).
  2. According to the article, what is causing the decline in rice producers? Options were (a) producers’ aging and (b) young people leaving agriculture. Correct answer was (a).

The second article, “Could rice cultivation in the plains become impossible? Extreme heat exceeds optimal temperatures,” appeared in Asahi Shimbun on October 15, 2025 (morning edition, Mie regional section, p. 25). A Mie University research group warned that further warming could restrict rice cultivation to particular areas of the prefecture. The excerpt also described shrinking irrigation channels under acreage reduction policies and the need to reorganize farmland and water use.

  1. According to the article, how would further warming affect rice cultivation in Mie Prefecture? Options were (a) rice could be grown only in particular areas and (b) rice cultivation would become completely impossible. Correct answer was (a).
  2. According to the article, what has shrunk in Mie Prefecture under acreage reduction policies? Options were (a) irrigation channels essential for rice cultivation and (b) the rice distribution network. Correct answer was (a).
6.2.1.2. Positive condition

The first article, “Expectations of lower rice prices as supply and demand ease,” appeared in Nihon Keizai Shimbun on November 11, 2025 (morning edition, p. 23). The excerpt reported an expected increase in the 2025 rice harvest to its highest level in nine years. It described expectations of lower prices and easing supply and demand, reflected in a decline in the outlook index.

  1. According to the article, the 2025 rice harvest would reach its highest level in how many years? Options were (a) three years and (b) nine years. Correct answer was (b).
  2. According to the article, what does the 10-point decline in the outlook index from the previous month mean for supply and demand? Options were (a) easing and (b) tightening. Correct answer was (a).

The second article, “Growing interest in upland rice cultivation in eastern Hokkaido,” appeared in Asahi Shimbun on October 15, 2025 (morning edition, Hokkaido regional section, p. 27). The excerpt described successful trials of upland rice and stable harvests in a region historically considered unsuitable for rice cultivation. A rise of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius in average spring and summer temperatures over approximately 40 years had made the climate more suitable.

  1. According to the article, which crop produced an unexpectedly abundant harvest in trials in eastern Hokkaido? Options were (a) upland rice and (b) paddy rice. Correct answer was (a).
  2. According to the article, why can rice now grow normally in the Tokachi region? Options were (a) a rise of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius in average temperatures and (b) land improvements for use as paddy fields. Correct answer was (a).

6.2.2. Exclusions

Responses were excluded in the order shown in Table 6. We dropped every response whose ID or IP address appeared more than once because we could not tell which response was valid (6 cases). We excluded 39 participants who did not agree to participate; they were redirected to the end screen and gave no responses. Based on responses to comprehension checks, we excluded 246 participants with at least one wrong answer to the four items: 100 from the negative prospects condition and 146 from the positive prospects condition. We also inspected response duration. The shortest response took 70 seconds; because the survey was short and these participants passed all comprehension checks, no response was excluded due to short response duration.

Before reading the articles, participants reported their household size, whether they were the main buyer of food in the household, how often per week they cooked and ate rice, and how much rice they cooked at a time. All five household variables were available for 235 participants (139 negative, 96 positive); 49 participants were omitted from the adjusted analyses. We entered the five variables as numeric covariates, with main buyer coded 1 for yes and 0 for no. Separate OLS models estimated condition differences in subjective prospects and each behavioral intention. Partial Pearson correlations used residuals after adjusting both variables for the same five covariates, pooled over news conditions; confidence intervals used Fisher’s transformation with five covariates. All t tests were two-sided; p values were unadjusted for multiple comparisons. The negative condition remained associated with more negative subjective prospects and higher private information-sharing intention, but the adjusted differences in purchase intention and public information-sharing intention were not statistically significant. More negative subjective prospects remained associated with purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, but not with public information-sharing intention (Table 8).

6.2.4. Behavioral variables

Expected structure. We had designed the items expecting the observation context, direct or indirect observation, to separate the items, and the sharing items to form one factor. Neither happened: purchase items from both contexts loaded on one factor, and sharing split into private and public information-sharing intentions.

Promax rotation. The promax solution gave the same three factors as the varimax solution. The factor correlations were .56 between purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, .18 between private and public information-sharing intention, and −.01 between purchase intention and public information-sharing intention. 6.2.8. Sharing after direct and indirect observation

Averaging the two items about private information-sharing intention within each observation context, participants were more willing to share a shortage they had observed directly (M = 2.96, SD = 0.95) than one they had observed indirectly in an SNS post (M = 2.69, SD = 0.95; t[283] = 5.85, p < .001, \(d_z\) = 0.35). The two composites were strongly correlated (r = .68). After rescaling both means to 0–1, sharing after indirect observation was 87% of sharing after direct observation. The difference did not depend on the condition: it was 0.32 in the negative prospects condition and 0.19 in the positive prospects condition (Welch’s t[262] = 1.43, p = .155, d = 0.17).

6.3. Study 2

6.3.1. Exclusions

During data collection, Qualtrics did not count responses with a wrong answer in the attention checks toward the planned sample of 500. As preregistered, we closed the survey once the counted responses reached 500, and participants who had already started were allowed to finish, which gave 1,028 raw responses. Responses were excluded by the preregistered rules, in the order shown in Table 13. Six attention checks were embedded in the observation context blocks and at the end of the survey: three asked whether the participant had looked at the image, two asked for a specified answer, and one asked whether the participant had read the questions carefully. A last check for a repeated participant ID or IP address, not in the preregistration, excluded no response.

6.3.2. Robustness checks

Number of factors. As in Study 1, we kept the three factors with eigenvalues greater than 1; the fourth and fifth eigenvalues of the item correlation matrix were 0.83 and 0.69.

Promax rotation. Every item loaded highest on its preregistered factor in both the varimax solution (purchase intention .67–.81, private information-sharing intention .72–.78, public information-sharing intention .76 and .90) and the promax solution. The promax factor correlations were .48 between purchase intention and private information-sharing intention, .44 between private and public information-sharing intention, and .07 between purchase intention and public information-sharing intention. [PLACEHOLDER: promax loading table.]

6.3.3. Exploratory analyses

Commodity. Subjective prospects were more negative for laundry detergent (M = 3.06, SD = 0.60) than for toilet paper (M = 2.85, SD = 0.70; t[504] = 3.71, p < .001, d = 0.32). Purchase intention was higher for toilet paper (M = 3.56, SD = 0.80) than for laundry detergent (M = 3.33, SD = 0.87; t[534] = 3.23, p = .001, d = 0.28), while private information-sharing intention, public information-sharing intention, and crisis concern did not differ (p \(\ge\) .114). Because subjective prospects differed between commodities, the preregistered exploratory plan called for commodity-specific correlations. They were similar for both commodities: for toilet paper (n = 257), r = .21 (purchase intention), .19 (private information-sharing intention), and .16 (public information-sharing intention); for laundry detergent (n = 279), r = .20, .21, and .24 (all p \(\le\) .009).

Crisis context. Three exploratory items asked how concerned participants were about the oil-supply situation, how much it would affect their daily shopping, and how long it would last (5-point scales; M = 3.91, SD = 0.84, \(\alpha\) = .67). Concern about the crisis was related to subjective prospects about the commodity (r = .17, p < .001), to purchase intention (r = .26, p < .001), and to private information-sharing intention (r = .18, p < .001), but not to public information-sharing intention (r = −.05, p = .255). In regressions with commodity, subjective prospects, crisis context and their interaction (predictors mean-centered), both subjective prospects and crisis context predicted purchase intention (b = 0.21 and 0.24, both p < .001) and private information-sharing intention (b = 0.25 and 0.18, both p < .001). For public information-sharing intention, only subjective prospects did (b = 0.27, p < .001; crisis b = −0.08, p = .061). The interaction was not significant for any outcome (all p \(\ge\) .222).

6.3.4. Sharing after direct and indirect observation

Averaging the two items about private information-sharing intention within each observation context, participants were more willing to share a shortage they had observed directly (M = 3.01, SD = 1.00) than one they had observed indirectly in an SNS post (M = 2.87, SD = 1.01; t[535] = 4.47, p < .001, \(d_z\) = 0.19). The two composites were strongly correlated (r = .75). After rescaling both means to 0–1, sharing after indirect observation was 93% of sharing after direct observation. [PLACEHOLDER: test whether the difference between direct and indirect observation depends on subjective prospects.]

6.4. Simulation

6.4.1. Depletion time at all rewiring probabilities

Figure 11 shows mean depletion time for every rewiring probability we ran: 0%, 0.1%, 0.2%, 0.3%, 0.5%, 0.7%, 1%, 1.5%, 2%, 3%, 5%, and 10%. The region of fast depletion first appeared at 0.2% and grew steadily with rewiring.

Figure 11: Mean depletion time (steps) across reaction sensitivity (\(s\)) and firsthand information sharing probability (\(p^{\text{S1}}\)), in steps of .05, at all rewiring probabilities (\(p^{\text{RW}}\)). Same gray scale as Figure 9. Each cell shows the mean of 50 matched runs.

6.4.2. Smoother reaction curve

To check that the main results do not depend on the step-like reaction curve (\(g = 20\)), we repeated the heatmaps with a smooth curve (\(g = 1\) and \(g = 2\)). The results were almost the same (Figure 12): without rewiring there was no fast region, any rewiring opened a fast region in the upper-right corner, and higher rewiring shifted the boundary toward lower reaction sensitivity and firsthand information sharing probability. The only visible difference was a slightly wider boundary at \(g = 1\).

Figure 12: Mean depletion time (steps) at sigmoid steepness \(g = 20\), 2, and 1, at selected rewiring probabilities (\(p^{\text{RW}}\), columns). Each cell shows the mean of 40 runs matched to the robustness sweep seeds, whereas the main text uses 50 runs.

6.5. Literature Review Check

Temporary section for discussion with the supervisor (draft, 2026-11-23; remove or rewrite before submission). Sources, extraction notes, and every number are traced in thesis/lit_review_scarcity_check.org; data and figures are rebuilt by scripts/lit_review_check.py.

6.5.1. Search and corpus

We built the panic-buying corpus using two complementary searches. First, a seeded citation-network search in a local OpenAlex database started from 10 seed papers (5 key studies and 5 reviews), screened 13,910 linked works using a written codebook, and retained 792 works after two expansion rounds and a title check. Second, a keyword search using (“panic buy*” OR “panic purchas*” OR “crisis stockpil*”) returned 588 records in Scopus, 410 in Web of Science, and 1,431 in OpenAlex; removing duplicates left 1,490 papers, of which 767 were screened as relevant. Merging both sets yielded 1,049 unique papers (503 found by both searches, 264 by the keyword search only, and 282 by the citation search only).

6.5.2. COVID-19 and other crises

Of the 1,049 papers, 684 (65.2%) examine COVID-19, 128 (12.2%) examine another named crisis, and 237 (22.6%) name no specific crisis (mostly theory, reviews, and general surveys). Among papers naming a crisis, 84.2% focus on COVID-19. Before 2020, the corpus contains 86 papers in total. The COVID-19 share peaked at 88% in 2020 and declined to 41% in 2025 (Figure 13).

Figure 13: Panic-buying papers in the review corpus by publication year and crisis studied (n = 1,047; two papers without a publication year omitted; 2026 covers through November 10). Labels show the COVID-19 share for years with at least 40 papers. Crisis categories follow the literature-review dashboard classification of each paper’s event description or title.
